iambic.e: From Middle French iambique, from Late Latin ïambicus, from Ancient Greek ἰαμβικός (iambikós), from ἴαμβος (íambos) + -ικός (-ikós).

iceberg.x: The Titanic hit an iceberg and sank.

icebreaker.e: From ice + breaker, in the figurative sense from the expression to break the ice.
icebreaker.x: My father's Bonneville was cutting its way toward us like an icebreaker moving through my whole state of consciousness.

icing.x: The Cessna pilots reported that moderate icing was present between 13,000 and 4,000 feet in the cloud layers.

iconic.e: From Late Latin īconicus, from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). By surface analysis, icon + -ic.
iconic.x: For younger musicians, Coltrane’s death became one of those iconic events that stays vividly in the mind.

iconoclast.e: Borrowed from French iconoclaste and its etymon Medieval Latin īconoclastēs, from Medieval Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, literally “image breaker”).

iconoclastic.x: Many of Thomas Hardy's works were considered iconoclastic in his day.

iconography.x: The hundredodd pages of photographs provide superb iconography of artistic collaboration and its rewards.

idealist.e: From French idéaliste, from Late Latin idealis (“ideal”), from Latin idea (“idea”), equivalent to ideal + -ist.

identifiable.x: I don't know where he was from because he had no identifiable accent.

identification.x: In many network protocols, identification is complemented by authentication.

identifier.x: The source stated that the alleged victims wanted the paperwork released after the settlement, but with names and identifiers removed.

ideological.x: There are economists from all over the ideological spectrum.

ideologue.e: Borrowed from French idéologue. By surface analysis, ideo- + -logue. First attested in the 19th century.

ideology.e: Borrowed from French idéologie, from idéo- + -logie (equivalent to English ideo- + -logy). Cognate with, but not derived from, idea.
ideology.x: A dictatorship bans things, that do not conform to its ideology, to secure its reign.

idiocy.x: The administrators, growing tired of such idiocy, put a new policy in place.

idiom.e: From Middle French idiome, and its source, Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “a peculiarity, property, a peculiar phraseology, idiom”), from ἰδιοῦσθαι…
idiom.x: In English, idiom requires the indefinite article in a phrase such as "she's an engineer", whereas in Spanish, idiom forbids it.

idiomatic.e: From Ancient Greek ἰδιωματικός (idiōmatikós, “related to an idiom”), from ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “idiom”).
idiomatic.x: The inclusion or omission of definite articles follows idiomatic norms in each language and depends on context and intent.

idiopathic.e: From idio- + -pathic. First appears c. 1669, in the publications of William Simpson.

idiosyncrasy.e: First attested in 1604, in modern sense since 1665, from Ancient Greek ἰδιοσυγκρασία (idiosunkrasía, “one’s own temperament”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one’s own”) + σύν (sún…
idiosyncrasy.x: Every village has its idiosyncrasy, its constitution, often its own code of morality.

idiosyncratic.e: From idiosyncrasy + -ic. By surface analysis, idio- + syn- + -cratic.
idiosyncratic.x: It was no merely idiosyncratic experience, for the youth had the same: it was love!

idiotic.x: Everyone else shifted uncomfortably as this guy continued his derisive laughter and proclaimed my quest the most idiotic thing he'd heard in his life.

idleness.e: From Middle English ydelnesse, from Old English īdelnes, from Proto-West Germanic *īdlanassī, equivalent to idle + -ness.

idolater.e: From Middle English ydolatrer, from Middle French idolatre, from Latin idololatra. Displaced native Old English dēofolġielda (literally “devil worshiper”).
idolater.x: You who can smash the idols, do so with a good courage; but do not be too fierce with the idolaters,—they worship the best thing they know.

idolatrous.x: Once Robert Smellie found her in a ruinous kirk on the Lang Muir, where of old the idolatrous rites of Rome were practiced.

idolatry.e: Inherited from Middle English ydolatrie, from Old French idolatrie, from Ecclesiastical Latin īdōlatrīa, from Late Latin īdōlolatrīa, from Ancient Greek εἰδωλολατρίᾱ…

idyll.e: From Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion), from diminutive of εἶδος (eîdos, “form, shape”).

idyllic.x: My fellow-creatures, from whom I was thus separated, began to assume idyllic virtue and beauty in my memory.

iftar.x: Iftars can be social events, where people congregate to eat and socialize.

igloo.x: General James Walsh signalled Strategic Air Command that the B-47 tore apart the igloo and knocked about 3 mark sixes.

igneous.x: The stone had an igneous appearance.

ignite.e: From Latin ignītus, past participle of igniō, ignire (“to set on fire, ignite”), from Latin ignis (“fire”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥gʷnis, and thus related to…
ignite.x: Their blend of concert harp, vibes, bass and Latin percussion ignited much of the audience.

ignition.x: Put the key in the ignition and turn it right.

ignoble.e: Borrowed from Middle French ignoble, from Latin ignōbilis, from in- (“not”) + gnōbilis, later nōbilis (“noble”).
ignoble.x: A base, ignoble mind, / That mounts no higher than a bird can soar.

ignominious.e: From Late Middle English ignominious (“disgraceful, shameful”), from Middle French ignominieux (modern French ignominieux), or from its etymon Latin ignōminiōsus…
ignominious.x: The time when the pseudovirtuous men and women die a painful and ignominious death has yet to come.

ignominy.e: Borrowed from French ignominie, from Latin ignōminia, from ig- (“not”) + nomen (“name”) (prefix assimilated form of in-).
ignominy.x: Bradly came out from hiding with a dyspeptic grunt, too depressed by ignominy to send a curse after the old woman.

ignoramus.e: After the ignorant lawyer Ignoramus, the titular character in the 1615 play Ignoramus by the English playwright George Ruggle.
ignoramus.x: “The cost of appearing with this bloviating ignoramus is obvious, it seems to me,” he said on “This Week,” the ABC News program.

ignorance.e: From Middle English ignoraunce, ignorance, from From Old French ignorance, from Latin ignōrantia. By surface analysis, ignor(e) + -ance.
ignorance.x: She shows total ignorance about the topic at hand.

ignorant.e: From Old French ignorant, from Latin ignōrāns (“unaware, unknowing”). By surface analysis, ignore + -ant.
ignorant.x: The ignorant peasant, without fault, is greater than the philosopher with many; for what is genius or courage without an heart?

iguana.e: Borrowed from Spanish iguana, from Taíno *iwana.
iguana.x: Marine iguanas line the shores of the islands, and are usually seen sprawled over lava rocks near the sea.

ikebana.e: From Japanese 生け花 (ikebana, literally “living flowers”).

ileum.e: Via Medieval Latin from Latin ilia.

ilium.e: Borrowed from Latin īlium (“lower abdomen”), from īle (“flank”).

illegality.e: From French illégalité, equivalent to il- + legality or illegal + -ity.
illegality.x: The criminal was aware of the illegality of his act.

illegally.x: He received a ticket for illegally parking next to a fire hydrant.

illegitimate.e: First attested in 1536, from Latin illēgitimus, most likely an adapted borrowing of Middle French illegitime, equivalent to il- + legitimate, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and…

illicit.e: Borrowed from French illicite, from Latin illicitus, from in- (“not”) + licitus (“allowed, permitted”), from licet (“it is allowed”). By surface analysis, il- + licit.
illicit.x: The bigamous marriage, while illicit, was not invalid.

illiteracy.x: Illiteracy is widespread in certain areas of the country.

illiterate.e: First attested in 1425–1475, in Middle English; from Middle English illiterat(e) (“uneducated, ignorant of Latin”), borrowed from Latin illīterātus, illitterātus…
illiterate.x: About half of the population in Ethiopia is illiterate.

illogical.x: I received an illogical reply and that left me standing there feeling confused.

illuminate.e: From Middle English illuminaten, borrowed from Latin illūminātus, perfect passive participle of illūminō (“lighten, light up, show off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)…
illuminate.x: A light that is one foot away from the subject's face will completely illuminate the face, but leave the rest of the body softer and darker.

illumination.x: The room was filled with soft illumination from the candles.

illusion.e: From Old French illusion, from Latin illūsiō, from illūdere, from in- (“at, upon”) + lūdere (“to play, mock, trick”). Displaced native Old English dwimmer.
illusion.x: We saw what looked like a tiger among the trees, but it was an illusion caused by the shadows of the branches.

illusory.e: Borrowed from Middle French illusorie (modern French illusoire), derived from Latin illūsōrius (“mocking, ironical”).

illustrate.x: We illustrate our definitions by including quotations or simple examples.

illustration.e: Borrowed from Middle French illustration, from Latin illūstrātiō, from illūstrō (“to illustrate”). By surface analysis, illustrate + -ion.
illustration.x: The illustration showing the water cycle made it much easier to understand for the children.

illustrator.x: Mary is one of the best illustrators of children's books in the country.

illustrious.e: From Latin illūstris (“bright, shining; distinguished, prominent, illustrious”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, to denote possession or presence of a…

imaginable.e: From Middle English ymaginable, from Latin imāginābilis; equivalent to imagine + -able.
imaginable.x: While running, they were exposed to the most hideous bespawling imaginable.

imaginary.e: From Middle English ymaginarie, ymagynary, from Latin imāginārius (“relating to images, fancied”), from imāgō, equivalent to imagine + -ary.
imaginary.x: Wilt thou add to all the griefs I suffer / Imaginary ills and fancied tortures?

imaginative.e: From Middle English ymagynatif, from Middle French imaginatif, from Medieval Latin imāginātīvus. By surface analysis, imagine + -ative.
imaginative.x: No doubt kibitzers are highly imaginative. How else could they see wins and brilliant combinations that do not exist?

imago.e: From Latin imāgō. Doublet of image. Compare typologically a Russian term for coordinate larva: личи́нка (ličínka) (akin to лик (lik)).

imbalance.x: The growing imbalances between the rich and poor first lead to more crime.

imbibe.e: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also…
imbibe.x: Without its sting, the common yellowjacket would be unable to steal ham from our sandwich or imbibe the sweet juice from our peach.

imbue.e: From Latin imbuō (“wet, moisten”). Compare imbibe.
imbue.x: The shirt was imbued with his scent.

imitate.e: Borrowed from Latin imitātus, perfect active participle of imitor (“to copy, portray, imitate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French imiter.
imitate.x: A wave simulator in the tank can re-enact tsunamis and northeasters, and imitate wave conditions from midocean.

imitation.e: From Middle English imitacioun, from Middle French imitacion, from Old French imitacion, from Latin imitatio.

imitator.e: From French imitateur, derived from Latin imitātor, equivalent to imitate + -or.

immaterial.e: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English immaterial, inmateriall (“incorporeal.
immaterial.x: Some believe that because ghosts are immaterial, they can pass through walls.

immature.e: From Middle French immature. Partially displaced unripe, from Old English unrīpe (“unripe, immature”).
immature.x: You're only young once, but you can be immature the rest of your life.

immaturity.x: His constant joking showed his immaturity.

immerse.e: Borrowed from Latin immersus, from immergō, from in + mergō.
immerse.x: The sculptor immersed himself in anatomic studies.

immersion.e: From late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin immersiō, immersiōnem (“dipping”).
immersion.x: She left the immersion on all the time, while I had been reared under pain of death to turn it off as soon as the bathwater was heated.

immigrant.e: From Latin immigrans, present active participle of immigrāre (“to migrate into”), from in- (“into”) + migrāre (“to migrate”).
immigrant.x: Approximately 1.5 million Mexicans are descendants of Irish immigrants.

immigrate.e: From Latin immigratus, past participle of immigro (“remove, move into”).
immigrate.x: He knows hardship. He has experienced life in a cold-water flat in Moldova before he immigrated to the States.

immigration.x: It took ages to get through immigration last time.

imminent.e: From the present participle of Latin imminēre (“to overhang”), from mineō ("to project, overhang"), related to minae (English menace) and mons (English mount).
imminent.x: “Iran posed no imminent threat to our nation, and it is clear that we started this war due to pressure from Israel and its powerful American lobby.”

immobile.e: From Old French immobile, from Latin immōbilis, equivalent to im- + mobile.

immobility.e: From Middle French immobilité, equivalent to immobile + -ity.
immobility.x: See how he still covers his face with his hands when he sees me and his immobility and fixed stare are often evident.

immobilize.e: From French immobiliser, equivalent to immobile + -ize.
immobilize.x: It is best to immobilize the injury until a doctor can examine it.

immortalise.e: From immortal + -ise. Perhaps modelled on Middle French immortaliser.
immortalise.x: His heroic deeds were immortalised in song and tale.

immortality.e: From Middle English immortalitee, immortalite, from Old French immortalité, from Latin immortālitās. Morphologically immortal + -ity.
immortality.x: In Greek mythology, Tithonus was granted immortality but not eternal youth.

immovable.e: From Middle English immevable, immoveable. Equivalent to im- + movable.
immovable.x: I pleaded with him not to resign, but he was immovable.

immune.x: As a diplomat, you are immune from prosecution.

immunization.e: From French immunisation. Coined by Albert Calmette. Equivalent to immunize + -ation or immune + -ization.
immunization.x: Immunization against influenza is important for all child-care workers.

immunize.e: From French immuniser, equivalent to immune + -ize.
immunize.x: It is now clear that the brevity of an indecent broadcast – be it word or image – cannot immunize it from FCC censure.

immutable.e: From Middle English immutable, from Latin immūtābilis (“unchangeable”); im- + mutable.
immutable.x: The government has enacted an immutable law.

impale.e: From Middle French, from Medieval Latin impālāre, from Latin palus, whence also pale.

impart.e: From Middle English imparten, borrowed from Middle French impartir, empartir, from Late Latin impartiō, impertiō, from im- (“in”) + Latin partiō (“divide”).
impart.x: Did not Mazzini impart his spirit to divided Italy, and make her one?

impartial.e: Borrowed from Middle French impartial. See im- + partial.

impartiality.e: From Middle French impartialité. By surface analysis, impartial + -ity = im- + partial + -ity.

impassable.x: When the beach became impassable, as at high tide, they drove a sandy track behind the dunes.

impasse.x: "Young man, this town is at a bit of an impasse. If you have any suggestion that might help, now would be the time to voice it."

impassive.e: From im- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + passive (“which is, or is capable of being, acted on; (obsolete) which suffers, or may suffer, pain, death, etc.”, adjective).

impatience.e: Inherited from Middle English impacience, from Old French impacience (modern French impatience), from Latin impatientia. By surface analysis, im- + patience.

impatient.e: From Old French impacient (modern French impatient), from Latin impatiēns. By surface analysis, im- + patient.
impatient.x: She dances when she becomes impatient.

impatiently.x: Stella was waiting impatiently for the delivery to come.

impeach.e: From Middle English empechen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman empecher, from Old French empeechier (“to hinder”), from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter”).
impeach.x: These ungracious practices of his sons did impeach his journey to the Holy Land.

impeachment.e: From Middle English empechement (“hindrance, impediment, obstacle, obstruction; legal accusation or charge; act of calling into question or discrediting.
impeachment.x: And here is as great an adventure as ever I heard of, and here, if we turn back, no little impeachment of all our honours.

impeccable.e: From Middle French impeccable, from Latin impeccabilis (“not liable to sin”), from im- (“not”) + peccare (“to err, to sin”).
impeccable.x: He grew up in Norway, but he writes impeccable English.

impeccably.x: The great pianist was a prolific composer, who wrote impeccably for the piano.

impedance.e: From impede + -ance. In sense 2 and sense 3 it was coined by English mathematician and physicist Oliver Heaviside in 1886.

impede.e: Borrowed from Latin impediō (“to shackle”), from pēs (“foot”) (compare pedestrian). First attested use as a verb was in William Shakespeare's Macbeth, see quotations.
impede.x: The human-machine imbalance made Sellers concerned that the modern thirst for AI-powered optimization was starting to impede human interaction.

impediment.e: From Middle English impediment, borrowed from Latin impedimentum.
impediment.x: Thus far into the bowels of the land Have we marched on without impediment.

impel.e: From Middle English impellen, borrowed from Latin impellō.

impending.x: I have no time right now because of an impending paper submission deadline.

imperceptible.e: Inherited from Middle English imperceptible, from Middle French imperceptible and its etymon Medieval Latin imperceptibilis. By surface analysis, im- + perceptible.
imperceptible.x: We all missed the imperceptible shake of his head as he tried to warn us without being seen.

imperfect.x: Why, then, your other senses grow imperfect.

imperfection.e: From Old French imperfeccion, from Latin imperfectiōnem, accusative of imperfectiō, from in- + perfectiō. By surface analysis, im- + perfection.
imperfection.x: You can accept your imperfection or try to improve.

imperious.e: From Latin imperiōsus (“mighty, powerful”), from imperium (“command, authority, power”).
imperious.x: She was quick, beautiful, imperious, while he was quiet, slow, and misty.

impermeable.e: Apparently from im- + permeable. Compare French imperméable, from Latin impermeābilis, from im- + permeābilis (“permeable”).

impersonal.e: From French impersonnel, from Latin impersōnālis, from im- (“not”) + persōnālis (“personal”), equivalent to im- + personal.
impersonal.x: The verb “rain” is impersonal in sentences like “It’s raining.”

impertinence.e: Borrowed from Middle French impertinence, from impertinent (“impertinent”); by surface analysis, im- + pertinent.
impertinence.x: The musical has always had a lightness of touch, an impertinence that resembles gay humor.

impertinent.e: Inherited from Middle English impertinent, from Middle French impertinent, from Old French impertinent, from Latin impertinēns; by surface analysis, im- + pertinent.

impervious.e: From Latin impervius (“that cannot be passed through”), from in- (“not”) + pervius (“letting things through”).
impervious.x: The man was completely impervious to the deception we were trying.

impetuous.e: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).
impetuous.x: But it was natural, that the impetuous, restless young artist should incline more to excess of strength than of delicacy in his playing.

impetus.e: Borrowed from Latin impetus (“a rushing upon, an attack, assault, onset”), from impetō (“to rush upon, attack”), from in- (“upon”) + petō (“to seek, fall upon”).
impetus.x: The outbreak of World War II in 1939 gave a new impetus to receiver development.

impish.x: "That's true, I did," Kate admitted, with an impish grin. "How did it look?"

implacable.e: From Middle English implācāble (“immitigable, unappeasable”) from Old French implacable (“harsh, unrelenting.
implacable.x: The battleships Washington and South Dakota pushed through the sea with an implacable ease.

implement.e: Borrowed from Late Latin implēmentum (“a filling up”), from Latin impleō (“to fill up”).
implement.x: It’s a good thought, but it will be a difficult thing to implement.

implementation.x: Now that the requirements are complete we can move on to implementation.

implication.x: Dumping waste in the river will have serious implications for the environment.

implicit.e: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.
implicit.x: Poets often leave behind an implicit message within their words.

implore.e: PIE word *h₁én The verb is borrowed from Middle French implorer (modern French implorer (“to beg, plead, implore”)), or directly from its etymon Latin implōrāre, the…
implore.x: And giue me leaue, / And doe not ſay 'tis Superſtition, that / I kneele, and then implore her Bleſſing.

imply.e: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”).
imply.x: When I state that your dog is brown, I am not implying that all dogs are brown.

impolite.e: Learned borrowing from Latin impolītus. Equivalent to im- + polite.

import.e: From Middle English importen, from Old French emporter, importer, from Latin importō (“bring in from abroad, import”, verb), from in (“in, at, on.

importer.x: India is the world's biggest importer of gold.

impose.e: The verb is derived from Late Middle English imposen (“to place, set.
impose.x: Sanctions were imposed on the country that had made an unprovoked attack on its neighbour.

imposing.x: The castle was an imposing sight on the hilltop.

impossibility.e: From Middle French impossibilité, from Latin impossibilitās. By surface analysis, im- + possibility and impossible + -ity.
impossibility.x: Meeting the deadline is an impossibility; there is no way we can be ready in time.

impossibly.x: The topology problem was impossibly difficult.

impostor.e: Borrowed from Middle French imposteur, respelled in the Latin manner; ultimately from Latin impositor, agent form of Latin imponere (“to impose”).

impotence.e: From Middle French impotence, from Latin impotentia.
impotence.x: O impotence of mind, in body ſtrong!

impotent.e: From Old French impotent, from Latin impotēns, from in- (expresses negation) + potēns (“powerful”).
impotent.x: A person smeared with the excrement of a mouse was rendered impotent, according to Pliny the Elder.

impoverish.e: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper…
impoverish.x: That exuberant crop quickly impoverishes any fertile soil.

imprecise.x: Rushdie oxymoronically notes that Hobson-Jobson ‘can be wonderfully imprecise at times’ (1985: 82).

impregnable.e: From Late Middle English imprenable, impregnable (“impossible to capture, impregnable”), from Old French imprenable (modern French imprenable (“impregnable”)), from im-…
impregnable.x: Jurgis got up, wild with rage; but the door was shut and the great castle was dark and impregnable.

impregnate.e: The adjective is first attested in 1540, the verb in 1605; borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate…
impregnate.x: I was impregnated at a clinic but don't know who the sperm donor is.

impregnation.e: From Middle English impregnacioun, from Old French impregnacion, in turn from Late Latin impregnatio.
impregnation.x: Earths and alkalies are simply metallic oxides; whilst a farther impregnation of these substances with oxygen produces an acid....

impressionable.x: I had never been an impressionable girl as far as men were concerned—I was not an impressionable woman.

imprint.x: Their footsteps left an imprint in the sand.

imprisonment.e: From Anglo-Norman emprisonement, from Old French emprisonnement. See imprison + -ment.
imprisonment.x: Human rights organisations say many experience imprisonment and beatings along the way.

improbable.e: Borrowed from Latin improbābilis. By surface analysis, im- + probable.
improbable.x: It's highly improbable that aliens abducted you.

impromptu.x: The party began with an impromptu rendition of “Happy Birthday”.

improper.e: From Middle French impropre, from Latin improprius (“not proper”), from in- + proprius (“proper”). By surface analysis, im- + proper.

improvement.e: From Anglo-Norman emprouwement. By surface analysis, improve + -ment.
improvement.x: Exercise is the chief source of improvement in all our faculties.

improvisation.x: He played a quick improvisation on the keyboard.

improvise.e: From French improviser; ultimately from Latin improvisus. Not related to improve.
improvise.x: He had no speech prepared, so he improvised.

imprudent.e: From Middle French imprudent, from Latin imprūdens (“not foreseeing, ignorant”), prefix im- (“not”) + prūdens (“foreseeing, skilled, judicious”).
imprudent.x: Here Her Majesty took a great dislike at the imprudent behavior of many of the Ministers and Readers.

impudence.e: From Middle French impudence, from Latin impudentia.

impudent.e: From Middle English impudent, originally meaning immodest, shameless, from Latin impudēns (“shameless”), ultimately from in- + pudere (“to feel shame”).
impudent.x: The impudent children would not stop talking in class.

impulse.e: Borrowed from Middle French impulser, from Latin impulsus.
impulse.x: c. 1715-1716, Samuel Clarke, letter to Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz All spontaneous animal motion is performed by mechanical impulse.

impulsive.e: Borrowed from Middle French impulsif, from Latin impulsivus.
impulsive.x: Poor men! poor papers! We and they / Do some impulsive force obey.

impunity.e: From Middle French impunité, from Latin impunitas, from impunis (“without punishment”).
impunity.x: I must not only punish but punish with impunity. A wrong is unredressed when retribution overtakes its redresser.

impure.e: From Middle French impur, from Latin impūrus.
impure.x: The impure gemstone was not good enough to be made into a necklace, so it was thrown out.

impurity.e: From impure + -ity. From Middle French impurité, from Latin impuritas.
impurity.x: Even animals in the Jewish system cause impurity only when they are dead.

impute.e: Borrowed from Middle French imputer, from Latin imputō (“to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute”).
impute.x: The teacher imputed the student's failure to his nervousness.

inability.e: From earlier inhability (“disqualification for office”), equivalent to in- + ability. Compare Middle French inhabilité, Medieval Latin inhabilitās.

inaction.e: From French inaction. Morphologically in- + action.
inaction.x: The school's inaction further sanctions this misbehavior.

inadequate.x: I had not yet seen Mrs. Kennedy. I wondered with what inadequate words I could try to console her.

inadvertent.x: We check everything because an inadvertent error could be disastrous.

inadvertently.x: 'Dear me! I may have inadvertently touched the handle,' said he.

inalienable.e: Borrowed around 1645 from French inaliénable, from in- + aliénable (“alienable”), equivalent to in- + alienable.
inalienable.x: An inalienable right is a right that cannot be given away nor taken away.

inane.e: From Latin inānis (“empty, vain, useless”), of unknown origin.
inane.x: One could say senseless, inane short-form media dominates social media as of the day.

inanimate.e: Inherited from Middle English inanimat(e), from Late Latin inanimātus, from Latin in- + animātus (“animated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
inanimate.x: Retired when her position was dissolved due to advances in inanimate automation.

inappropriate.x: It is inappropriate to burp at a formal dinner.

inattentive.x: He was inattentive in class and did not do well in his exams.

inject.e: From Latin iniectus, injectus, participle of iniciō, injiciō (“to throw in”), from in- + iaciō (“I throw”).

innovation.e: Borrowed from Middle French innovation, from Old French innovacion, from Late Latin innovatio, innovationem, from Latin innovo, innovatus.

inscribe.e: Borrowed from Latin īnscrībō, from in- (“upon”) and scrībō (“to write”).

inscription.x: The coin bears an inscription in Latin.

insect.e: Borrowed from Middle French insecte, from Latin īnsectum, from īnsectus (“cut into, cut up, with a notched or divided body”), from perfect passive participle of īnsecō…

interviewee.x: Both ‘no-op’ interviewees hold relatively stable identities as TG and offer interesting perspectives on trans repudiation from a TG standpoint.

interviewer.x: “I don't consider myself a nebbish,” Woody told interviewers early in his career, “but everyone else does.”

intestinal.e: From Latin intestīnālis. By surface analysis, intestine + -al.

intestine.e: From Latin intestīnum, neuter of intestīnus (“internal”), as Etymology 2, below.

intifada.e: Borrowed from Arabic اِنْتِفَاضَة (intifāḍa, “shaking off, uprising, insurrection”).

intimate.e: Borrowed from Latin intimātus, the perfect passive participle of intimō (“to put or bring into, to impress, to make familiar”) (see -ate (adjective forming suffix)), from…
intimate.x: He and his sister deeply valued their intimate relationship as they didn't have much else to live for.

intimidation.e: From intimidate + -ion. Compare French intimidation; perhaps modeled on it.

intolerable.e: Inherited from Middle English intolerable, borrowed from Middle French intolerable, from Latin intolerābilis. By surface analysis, in- + tolerable.
intolerable.x: It is an intolerable sound that sets spoons tinkling in saucers and windowpanes vibrating.

intolerance.e: Borrowed from French intolérance, itself from in- (“not”) + tolérance or borrowed from Latin intolerantia (“insolence, insufferableness; (very rare) intolerance”).
intolerance.x: Religious intolerance is a serious problem in Brazil.

intolerant.e: First attested in the first half of the 18th century; either borrowed from French intolérant (early 17th century) or from its source, Latin intolerāns.
intolerant.x: I am lactose-intolerant, so I can't drink milk.

intonation.e: From French intonation, from Medieval Latin intonatio, from intonō + -tiō.
intonation.x: In anxious expectation stood the crowd, When the shrill clarion's intonation loud Gave notice that the challenger drew nigh.

intoxicate.e: First attested in 1450, in Middle English; from Middle English intoxicaten, from intoxicat(e) (“(of a weapon or drug) smeared, anointed or filled with poison.

intoxication.x: He suffered acute intoxication from the combined effects of several drugs.

intractable.x: And I cannot but expect that this will repeatedly lead to the discovery that an initially intractable problem can be factored after all.

intramuscular.e: From Late Latin intramuscularis, from prefix intra-, "within", + musculum, "muscle".

intransigence.e: From French intransigeance, noun form of intransigeant, borrowed from Spanish intransigente at the end of the nineteenth century.
intransigence.x: The intransigence of both sides frustrated the negotiators.

intransigent.e: Borrowed from French intransigeant, from Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- (“un-, not”) + trānsigēns, present participle of trānsigō (“to come to an understanding”)…
intransigent.x: Don't waste your time trying to change his mind: he's completely intransigent.

intransitive.x: The word "drink" is a transitive verb in "they drink wine", but an intransitive one in "they drink often."

intravenous.x: Ikenna had typhoid and had been admitted at the hospital, receiving intravenous injections.

intrepid.x: Fewer than 70 years earlier, the intrepid James Cook in his ship Resolution had been the first explorer to cross the Antarctic Circle.

intricate.e: From Middle English intricat(e) (“entangled, intricate”), from Latin intrīcātus, perfect passive participle of intricō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
intricate.x: The architecture of this clock is very intricate.

intrigue.e: Borrowed from French intrigue, from Italian intricare, from Latin intrīcō (“to entangle, perplex, embarrass”). Doublet of intricate.
intrigue.x: His betrayal was the beginning of a complex intrigue intended to give him control of the company.

intrinsic.e: From Middle French intrinsèque, from Latin intrīnsecus (“on the inside, inwardly”), from *intrim, an assumed adverbial form of inter (“within”) + secus (“by, on the…
intrinsic.x: He was better qualified than they to estimate justly the intrinsic value of Grecian philosophy and refinement.

intrinsically.x: What cannot be commoditized because it is intrinsically inaccessible to commodification?

introduction.e: From Middle English introduccioun, introduccyon, borrowed from Old French introduction, itself a borrowing from Latin intrōdūctiōnem, accusative of Latin intrōdūctiō…
introduction.x: David was feeling groggy at his introduction to Sophie, and didn't remember her name.

introductory.e: Borrowed from Late Latin intrōductōrius, from Latin intrōductus.
introductory.x: He enrolled in an introductory wine-making course.

intrude.e: From Latin intrudere, from in- + trudere (“to thrust”).
intrude.x: The noise of machinery intruded on an otherwise quiet morning.

intrusion.e: From Middle English intrusioun, from Old French intrusion, from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from intrūdō, from Latin in- + trūdō.
intrusion.x: She viewed sales calls as an unwelcome intrusion.

intrusive.x: Did it ever cross your mind that he might find all those questions you ask intrusive?

intubate.e: From in- + tube + -ate (verb-forming suffix). First appears c. 1612 in the publications of Simon Sturtevant.
intubate.x: The doctor is about to intubate the patient's trachea.

intuition.e: From Middle French intuition, from Medieval Latin intuitiō (“a looking at, immediate cognition”), from Latin intueor (“to look at, consider”), from in- (“in, on”) + tueor…

intuitive.x: The intuitive response turned out to be correct.

inundate.e: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin inundātus, the perfect passive participle of inundō (“to flood, overflow”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- + undō…
inundate.x: The Dutch would sometimes inundate the land to hinder the Spanish army.

inundation.e: From Old French inundacion (“flood”) (French inondation), from Latin inundatio (“flood”), form of inundō (“to flood, overflow”) (English inundate).
inundation.x: Crescent City was considered to be at the highest risk of inundation before the arrival of the waves, the NWS said.

invade.x: Under some circumstances police are allowed to invade a person's privacy.

invader.x: The underroot tendril! We are at fault for giving the invader a path to Lady Brianna.

invalid.x: Your argument is invalid because it uses circular reasoning.

invalidate.e: First attested in 1649; borrowed from Middle French invalider, from invalide + -er. By surface analysis, in- + validate or invalid + -ate.
invalidate.x: The circuit court judge's ruling was invalidated by a superior judge.

invaluable.e: From in- + valuable (compare priceless). Piecewise doublet of unvaluable.

invasive.e: PIE word *h₁én The adjective is derived from Middle English invasif (“of a weapon: offensive”), from Middle French invasif, Old French invasif (“invasive”) (modern French…
invasive.x: It's wrong of me to ask such an invasive question when I keep so many secrets hidden from you.

invent.e: From Middle English inventen, borrowed from Old French inventer, from Latin inventus, perfect passive participle of inveniō (“come upon, meet with, find, discover”), from…
invent.x: After weeks of hard work, I invented a new way to alphabetize matchbooks.

invention.e: From Middle English invencion, invencioun, from Latin inventiō either directly or via Middle French invencion, from Latin invenīre (“to discover, find, invent”), from in-…
invention.x: My new invention will let you alphabetize your matchbook collection in half the usual time.

inventive.e: From Middle English inventif, inventyfe, borrowed from Old French inventif, borrowed from Medieval Latin inventivus. By surface analysis, invent + -ive.

inventor.e: Borrowed from Latin inventor. By surface analysis, invent + -or.
inventor.x: Thomas Edison was the inventor of the phonograph.

inventory.e: From Middle English inventorie, from Medieval Latin inventōrium, alteration of Late Latin inventārium, from Latin inveniō (“to find out”).
inventory.x: Due to an undersized inventory at the Boston outlet, customers had to travel to Providence to find the item.

invert.x: to invert a cup, the order of words, rules of justice, etc.

invest.e: Borrowed from Middle French investir or Medieval Latin investire, from Latin investio (“to clothe, cover”), from in- (“in, on”) + vestio (“to clothe, dress”), from vestis…
invest.x: We'd like to thank all the contributors who have invested countless hours into this event.

investigator.e: Attested in the mid‐16th century; from Latin investigator, from investigare, equivalent to investigate + -or.

inveterate.e: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1574; borrowed from Latin inveterātus (“of long standing, chronic”), perfect passive participle of inveterō and…
inveterate.x: In Montpelier, where this prison stands, the inveterate prejudice against prisoners has been swept away.

invigorate.e: First attested in 1646; borrowed from New Latin invigōrātus, perfect passive participle of invigōrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

invincibility.e: From Middle French invincibilité, from Latin invincibilitas.

invincible.e: From Middle French invincible, from Latin invincibilis (“unconquerable”), from in- (“not”) + vincibilis (“conquerable”), from vincere (“to conquer”).

inviolable.e: From Middle French inviolable, from Latin inviolābilis (“untouchable”), from violō (“violate”). Equivalent to in- + violable. Piecewise doublet of unviolable.
inviolable.x: But come, for thou, be ſure, ſhalt give account / To him who ſent us, whoſe charge is to keep / This place inviolable, and therefore theſe from harm.

invisibility.e: From Middle French invisibilité, from Latin invisibilitas.

invocation.e: From Middle English invocacioun, from Old French invocacion, from Latin invocatio, invocationem. Equivalent to invoke + -ation.

invoice.e: Borrowed from Middle French envois pl, plural of envoi, from the verb envoyer (“to send”). See also envoy.
invoice.x: I've already rendered the invoices for payment.

invoke.e: From Middle English *invoken, envoken, borrowed from Old French envoquer, from Latin invocāre (“to call upon”), itself from in- + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of invocate.
invoke.x: The envoy invoked the King of Kings's magnanimity to reduce his province's tribute after another drought.

involuntary.x: He found himself the involuntary witness in the trial.

involve.e: PIE word *h₁én From Late Middle English involven (“to cloud; to encumber; to envelop, surround; to ponder (something).
involve.x: My job involves forecasting economic trends.

invulnerable.e: From Middle French invulnérable, from Latin invulnerābilis, from vulnerābilis, from vulnerō (“to wound”), from vulnus (“wound”), equivalent to in- + vulnerable.
invulnerable.x: His gaze went to Hirken, who stood gloating behind invulnerable transparisteel.

irascible.e: From Middle English, from Old French irascible, from Late Latin īrāscibilis, from Latin īrāscī (“to be angry, enraged”) + -bilis. See also -ible.
irascible.x: I am naturally irascible, and if I could have shaken this negative gentleman vigorously, the relief would have been immense.

irate.e: From Latin īrātus (“angered, angry”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from īrāscor (“to be angry”), from īra (“anger, wrath”).

iridescent.e: Coined around 1800, from Latin iris, iridis (“rainbow”) + -escent.

iridium.x: Iridium is extremely rare on the surface of the earth but much more common in meteorites.

irksome.e: From Middle English irkesome, irksum, equivalent to irk + -some, or perhaps continuing (in altered form) from Old English weorcsum (“painful, hurtful”).
irksome.x: He has this irksome habit of racing up to red lights, so he has to brake heavily.

ironclad.x: Unlike the average vehicle, cash delivery vans are ironclad and almost unstoppable.

ironic.e: Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós). Compare Middle French, ironique, equivalent to irony + -ic.
ironic.x: It's somewhat ironic to have a wave of smog right on Earth Day.

ironically.x: My colleague ironically avoids doctors like the plague!

ironing.x: I really should make a start on the ironing soon.

ironmonger.e: From Middle English iremonger; equivalent to iron + monger.

ironworks.x: Many of its cottages were built for quarrymen when local workings provided limestone for the great 19th-century ironworks at Nantyglo.

irony.e: From Middle English hyrony, yreny, yrony, yrunny, equivalent to iron + -y.
irony.x: Irony, saying what it ne'er intends, Censures with praise, and speaks to foes as friends.

irradiation.e: From Middle French irradiacion, from Latin irradiatio. Morphologically irradiate + -ion.

irrational.e: From Latin irratiōnālis, from ir- + ratiōnālis.

irrationality.e: From irrational + -ity. May also be analyzed as ir- + rationality.

irreconcilable.e: Borrowed from Middle French irréconciliable, from Late Latin irreconciliābilis, from in- (“not”) + reconciliō (“to reconcile”) + -ābilis (“-able”).
irreconcilable.x: I amused myself by thinking that in his choice of books he showed pleasantly the irreconcilable sides of his fantastic nature.

irrefutable.e: From Late Latin irrefūtābilis, from ir- (“not”) + refūtābilis (“refutable”), from refūtō (“to refute”) + -bilis (“-able”), equivalent to ir- + refutable.
irrefutable.x: He had formed his mind by Helvetius, whose system he deemed irrefutable, and in whom alone he had faith.

irregular.e: From Middle English irreguler, from Old French irreguler, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin irrēgulāris, from in- + regularis, equivalent to ir- + regular.
irregular.x: Near by, where the crystal clear River Llugwy is crossed by a bridge, stands a small and ancient church built of massive, irregular boulders.

irregularity.e: From Middle French irrégularité, from Medieval Latin irregularitas. Morphologically irregular + -ity.

irrelevant.x: His comments were completely irrelevant to the discussion.

irreparable.e: From Middle French irréparable, from Old French, from Latin irreparabilis, equivalent to ir- + reparable.

irreplaceable.x: For some purposes lead is unique and, apparently, irreplaceable. Battery plates may be an example of this.

irreproachable.e: First attested in 1630. Borrowed from French irréprochable, from Middle French inreprochable. See also ir- + reproachable.

irrevocable.e: From Middle French irrévocable, from Latin irrevocabilis; equivalent to ir- + revoke + -able.
irrevocable.x: Firm and irrevocable is my doom Which I have pass'd upon her; she is banish'd.

irrigate.e: First attested in 1615; borrowed from Latin irrigātus, perfect passive participle of irrigō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
irrigate.x: We need to irrigate the land before we plant the crops.

irrigation.e: Borrowed from Middle French irrigation, from Latin irrigatio.

irritability.e: From Latin irritabilitās, equivalent to irritable + -ity.
irritability.x: We find a renitency in ourselves to ascribe life and irritability to the cold and motionless fibres of plants.

irritable.e: Borrowed from French irritable, from Latin irritabilis.

irritate.e: Borrowed from Latin irrītātus, perfect passive participle of irrītō (“excite, irritate, incite, stimulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
irritate.x: Thou scandalizest me and irritatest my nature as much as it possibly can be irritated.

irritated.x: She felt irritated by the constant noise.

irritation.e: Borrowed from Middle French irritation, from Latin irrītātiō, from irrītāre (“to excite”). By surface analysis, irritate + -ion.
irritation.x: What irritation causes you to be so moody?

ischemia.e: From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain.

islander.e: From island + -er. Displaced Middle English insulane (“islander”), from Latin īnsulānus (“islander”).

islet.e: From Middle French islette. By surface analysis, is(le) + -let.
islet.x: There is an islet on the other side of this body of water.

isolate.e: Back-formation from isolated, from French isolé, from Italian isolato, from Latin īnsulātus (whence also insulate), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).

isolated.e: A rendering into English of French isolé.
isolated.x: And while one isolated act of kindness may seem random, it can lead to much more.

isolation.e: First attested in 1800. From French isolation, from isolé, placed on an island (thus away from other people). Equivalent to isolate + -ion.
isolation.x: She lived her final year in complete isolation, not wanting to see anybody.

isometric.x: Superintendent, I was just, uh, stretching my calves on the windowsill. Isometric exercise! Care to join me?

isomorphic.x: The fact that different structures can be shown to be functionally isomorphic implies that they are analogous, not homologous.

isopod.e: From the taxonomic name Isopoda; by surface analysis, iso- + -pod.

isosceles.e: Borrowed from Latin īsoscelēs, from Ancient Greek ἰσοσκελής (isoskelḗs, “equal-legged”), from ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + σκέλος (skélos, “leg”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix).
isosceles.x: Upon each exterior side draw an Isosceles Triangle of 480 Fathoms.

isotope.e: From iso- (“equal”) + -tope (“place”), because the different isotopes of an element always occupy the same place in the periodic table.

isthmus.e: Borrowing from Latin isthmus (“a strip of land between two seas”), from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck, narrow passage”), possibly from εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “to go”).

italic.e: Named after the nation of Italy, as it was first used by an Italian printer, Aldo Manuzio, around 1500. Literally Italy + -ic.
italic.x: The text was impossible to read: every other word was underlined or in a bold or italic font.

itchy.e: From Middle English *yicchy, *ȝicchi, from Old English ġiċċiġ (“itchy”), equivalent to itch + -y.
itchy.x: Her heart kicked and an itchy burning in her throat made her swallow all her saliva away.

iteration.e: From Latin iterātiō, from iterō. Morphologically iterate + -ion.
iteration.x: The architect drafted several iterations of the floorplan before deciding on his final design.

ivory.e: From Middle English yvory, ivorie, from Anglo-Norman ivurie, from Latin eboreus (“in or of ivory”) adjective of ebur (“ivory”) (genitive eboris), from Demotic Egyptian yb…
